Hangberg on a knife's edge

By: Annalise Lubbe | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
When a fisher goes missing at sea during a police raid the locals of Hangberg take to the streets in protest. Carte Blanche investigate.

Summary:
It is cold winter’s morning in Hangberg, a fishing village on the outskirts of Hout Bay. From inside the church the last notes of “what a friend we have in Jesus” filters through the somber air. The Pastor prays for the return of a ‘missing son’ and lay hands on the family as they ask for a miracle to happen. It has been five days since Deurick van Blerk went missing at sea. In the icy winter waters of the Cape there is little hope now for a safe return.

“Please bring back our son,” ask the father, Edward van Blerk. “We still have hope that we will see our son alive,” he says.

26-Year-old Deurick van Blerk went missing on Friday night when he was out at sea catching crayfish with two fellow fishers. On the same night SAPS Water wing was out in full swing on an anti-poaching operation. They came across the boat, confiscated the crayfish and arrested two of the three fishers. In a statement issued by SAPS they were not clear if Van Blerk fell overboard or jumped. People are now speculating that perhaps he was shot at by the police and fell into the icy Cape waters.



Further information:
On Saturday morning, the NSRI and EMS choppers did a search for van Blerk but were later told to return to land when the weather turned nasty. On the same day Edward van Blerk filed a report for his missing son. He was told by the police that the search will only continue the following day.

On Sunday the search continued: the police sent out two jet skis and a rubber duck. “Why did they not send out proper big search boats like the ones they used on Friday night?”, says Ikram Halim, a representative of the Small Scale fishers. They are not serious about the search, he exclaims.

The community of Hangberg took to the streets in protest against the feeble attempt by the police. They set alight a fish factory, burned down one of DAFF’s offices and set a fishing boat alight in one of the streets. Eleven people were arrested.

On Monday the search continued. On Tuesday it was called off when the rubber duck ran out of petrol. On Wednesday afternoon the family was told that unless they have further leads, they will call of the search this Friday.

Behind the veil of protest is anger. Anger about the fact that they have been marginalised as fishers. Almost every second person living in Hangberg is a fisher. Over the years they have lost their quota as small scale fishers and can no longer make a living on what they are allowed to catch.
There are about 6 500 people living in Hangberg on the size of a postage stamp: cramped in and nowhere to expand. Most of the men here are fishers and have been living off the sea for generations. But due to DAFF cutting down on the amount of permits issued each year for crayfishing and abalone, cutting out a decent living has become impossible and poaching became the only way out.

Poaching is rife in the waters along the coast of Hout Bay. Stretching over several kilometres it is an impossible task to police the waters efficiently. Besides SAPS’ water wing, the City of Cape Town has their own Marine Law Enforcement task team patrolling the waters for illegal fishing activities. On any give clear day you will find poachers. The only way to spot them easily is with a drone. Here about 12 divers is out in full force diving out abalone.

But is the solution to work reactively and go after the poachers or should we not look at sustainable solutions that will be beneficial to both the small scale fishers, the commercial companies and most importantly our marine life.

Sustainability of our sea resources is vital for job creation: from pro bono fishers to commercial companies, protecting our marine resource is imperative for the future. Scientific studies has shown that the total allowable catch (TAC) for the West Coast rock lobster is at a level which will wipe out the crustaceans if drastic measures are not put in place to cut down the percentage of rock lobsters harvested each year from our seas.

The World Wide Fund for Nature South Africa (WWF-SA) is taking the Department of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries (DAFF) to court over its failure to safeguard the future of the special and all the fishers who depend on this valuable resource. Currently less that 2% of its pre-fished stock size, the the west coast rock lobster is in danger to be wiped out. Pedro Garcia, founder of the South African United Fishing Front (SAUFF) have been working with WWF to plead for the sustainable future of the rock lobster as this is directly related to the future of the artisans.
Following the protest in Hout Bay, Fisheries minister, Senzeni Zokwana has issued directives to senior officials to accelerate the process of allocating fishing rights in coastal communities. But why has it taken almost 10 years, says Halim, for them to sit up and taken notice? And is this not going to be another ploy to pacify the community when they have not made any serious attempt to help us since 2006.

Jacobus van Niekerk has been a fisher for 29 years. Every year his wife, Charmaigne fills in the form requesting for a small scale fishing permit. “I sit in the hall when they call out the names, but his name is never on the list”. “We have given up trying”. Jacobus is now working on a boat to make a living and he is just one of many disappointed fishers who have been sidelined by the government in the issuing of permits.

Our Story:
We tell the story behind the missing fisher: why poaching has become the only way out for the fishers of Hangberg.

We hear from the van Blerk family about losing a son; from the community about losing their dignity and from a poacher resorting to illegal fishing as the only way out. We put the government on the spot and ask why it is taking so long to allocate fishing rights to those who need it most; and hear from SAPS what really happened that night and get a perspective from the WWF on the sustainable future of the rock lobster and how it will impact the small scale fishers.

NOTES: The WWF – we need to script stronger that there is a huge threat that they are over quota
Is this only about rock lobster, what else are they fishing? Crayfish
Beautifully shot
Feels long – would reduce to 9 minutes
It needs better weaving.

SUGGESTION: At first the story feels like it’s about the shooting where Deurick was killed, then we say he is a poacher, then afterwards we explain the plight of the fishers and that Deurick and the fishers aren’t really poachers but they’ve had to resort to poaching.
Then we go back to Deurick’s family. Very difficult then to be sympathetic to Deurick when we first establish him as a poacher instead of a hard working fisher who got a raw deal because of gov regulations.
We shouldn’t start with the memorial shot, rather we set up the problem for fishers in Hangberg first and why they became poaochers, then we go to the killing of Deurick and the response from SAPS, then back to the issues of the fishers and the official DAFF response then end with Deurick’s dad.
Parts are repetitive because we already know he was excited to be a dad but we let both his dad and partner go on about it.
Amateur footage strap should stay on for longer – at least five seconds
SAPS response should be much earlier
Structure
Collage of Deurick is weird

Script:


FINAL SCRIPT: Hangberg on a knife’s edge
Producer: Annalise Lubbe / Presenter: MacFarlane Moleli
Date: 7 September 2018 / Duration: 10 minutes

V/O Hangberg, a traditional fishing community in Cape Town. It’s roughly six and a half thousand residents depend on the sea – catching crayfish, abalone and line fish. As the population grew and commercial fishing increased, fish stocks declined. Government efforts to license access to the ocean forced out traditional fishers. Many turned to poaching as a way out.
Ralph Warner: Fisher - My father was a fisherman; my grandfather had boats, a lot of rowing dinghies, so they were catching quotas; now where is the quotas now?
MacFarlane Moleli: So how does this make you feel? This is your life.

Ralph Warner: It’s make me feel sad. In Hangberg I have got four siblings to support. What must I do? So I turn to poaching.

V/O In 2005 a civic organisation took government to the equality court over its policies that excluded artisanal fishers. In 2007 the court ruled that interim rights must be given to small-scale fishers. The Department of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries or DAFF had to devise a policy that covered small-scale fishers. By 2012 the new policy was announced – but to date it has not been implemented. In Hangberg only 97 fishers, out of the hundreds in the area, have Interim Relief permits.

Neville Adonis: Fisher - You must go and catch the fish but you can’t catch the fish if you haven’t got a permit. I fill in my form, it’s in, come back, unsuccessful. All the fisherman, not me alone, all the fisherman, they are sick and tired.

Up natural sound: police shooting and firing rubber bullets.

V/O Unable to improve their lives when fishing quotas are poor, residents often protest in frustration over poor living conditions. The municipality has evicted fishers form illegal shacks – the only homes they can afford. There are sporadic and increasing, violent clashes between police and Hangberg residents.

Up audio:

V/O In August renewed unrest erupted after a 26-year old fisherman Durick van Blerk was allegedly shot at by police. Van Blerk disappeared at the sea. Like so many youngsters in Hangberg, Van Blerk had turned to poaching to try and improve his life.

UP audio: so you are looking to start a family now.

V/O His fiance, Cleo Adonis, is heavily pregnant.

MacFarlane Moleli: So Cleo this your home?

Cleo Adonis: Fiance - Yeh. This was the home me and Durick prepared before all this happened. As you can see we are still busy building and sorting out the house before the baby comes. He was very excited to become a dad, this will be his first child.

MacFarlane Moleli: What kind of boyfriend was he?

Cleo Adonis: He was very loving. He was my everything in my life. If I call him, Durick come and fetch me here. He would come immediately.

V/O Van Blerk’s father Edward was helping his son with electrical fittings in his new home.

Edward van Blerk: Father - Ek is besig om die huis maarwee hy besig is te help bou (I am busy helping him with the home he was building) Toe het ek vrydag die 10de het ek gegaan, het ek begin nou in die mure die snywerk doen sodat ons die plugs en pype in die muur kan sit. (On Friday the tenth I went there to cut into the walls to install the plugs and pipes)

Up audio boat sound

V/O That was the last time that Van Blerk saw his son. In the early hours of 11 August Van Blerk and two other men went out crayfishing around Hout Bay – illegally. Police were scouting for poachers – outside of crayfish season anyone in the water was a suspect. The police allegedly fired shots in their direction and Van Blerk went overboard

Edward van Blerk: Daar is rumours daar was geskiet maar ons het niks bewyse nie. (there are rumours that shots have been fired) ek is baie baie ontsteld vir die polisiemanne wat daar was (I am very upset about the police who were there), want die wet se as jy sien n persoon val in die water op see dan moet jy vir hom uit die water help, (because the law says that when you see a person falling in the sea then you have to help him out of the water) jy kan nie net hom daar los nie. (you can’t just leave him there)

V/O Van Blerk’s two friends were arrested for possession of illegal crayfish and brought to shore. Word got out about the alleged shooting.

MacFarlane Moleli: Wat se die ander twee manne van die ding? (What do the other two men say about this?)

Edward van Blerk: Die ander twee manne se op die boot van hulle was geskiet. (the other two men said they shot at the boat) Die een persoon se Durick het op hom gaan val (the one person said Durick fell on him) die ander se hy het net gesien Durick is in die water met sy hande in die lug (the other one said he saw Durick was in the water with his hands up in the air) want dit was mos nou donker gewees toe die nou gebeur het. (because it was obviously dark when it happened).

V/O When Van Blerk didn’t return from sea his family turned to the police, but they learned nothing about his disappearance. In the days that followed a number of search teams went out, including SAPS divers, the National Sea Rescue Institute and local fishers.

Up sound:

Link: Due to the anger and frustration of the fishing community they took to the streets in protests and also burnt down some government buildings. This is one of them.

V/O Protesters unleashed their anger on the Department of Fisheries – an employee’s house and car, as well as the station master’s office, were set alight. A warehouse was destroyed.

Up sound:

V/O We asked the police to explain what happened on the night Van Blerk went missing. They said they are not in a position to grant an interview as the Independent Police Investigation Directorate is investigating the police for attempted murder. IPID confirmed this. No arrest has been made yet.

MacFarlane Moleli: The reaction of the community is very angry about what has happened to the shooting of one of the fishers.

Ralph Warner: Fisher - The people must be angry because we don’t hunt with the gun the crayfish. We go out there to put food on our table. Why do they shoot the people? Why?

V/O Pedro Garcia represents small scale fishers on national level. Their primary objective is to restore justice and empower informal fishers.

Pedro Garcia: Co-chair Small Scale Collective - In 2007 the court ruled that a small scale policy be developed. It is now 12, 13 years and nothing has happened so you can imagine the frustrations that is on the ground. DAFF had failed our people. Make no mistake about that. They had allocated resources which were critically needed. They have allocated those resources to the bigger companies and to the near shore commercial.

V/O DAFF’s Craig Smith is responsible for the Small Scale Fishing policy.

MacFarlane Moleli: So Graig we met some small scale fishers that have been fishing all of their lives, they meet all the criteria and they have applied and said nothing has happened. They say the department has led them down.

Craig Smith - Director Small Scale Fisheries DAFF: For Western Cape, yes we have experienced delays. We haven’t got to the point of announcing the final list of fishers in western cape.

MacFarlane Moleli: When do you think it will be finalised?

Craig Smith: We are currently waiting for the minister to make the final decision on the list for western cape. One of the hiccups is with this national implementation the staff component is severely curtailed. We have only 8 staff in DAFF to implement this national programme.

MacFarlane Moleli: So would you not say the Department needs to work faster.

Craig Smith: There is no doubt that it needs to be expedited. The court case happened in 2007, we are eleven years after that particular court order and certainly we owe it to our communities to implement small scale fishing a lot quicker.

V/O Fishing rights only have value as long as there are fish in the sea. But in addition to the limited access to permits, small scale fishers have been dealt another blow. The World Wide Fund is taking DAFF to court over its apparent failure to safeguard the future of the West Coast Rock lobster. Dr. Theressa Frantz is head of their Environmental Programmes.

Dr Theressa Frantz - Head Environmental Programmes WWF-SA: We are extremely concerned about the status of the West Coast Rock Lobster resource. The global standard is 20%; we are at 2%. So by any standard we have already depleted this resource.

V/O DAFF has set the total allowable catch for South Africa for the West Coast Rock lobster at 1924 tonnes. Scientists say that’s more than double the amount that should be fished if stocks are to stabilise and recover.

Dr Theressa Frantz: So WWF is challenging the Department of Agriculture Forestry and Fisheries in court over the deputy director general’s decision for a total allowable catch that far exceeds the scientifically recommended level. The small scale fisheries collective has in fact come out in terms of our application and they understand the reason for sustainability of resource. While they recognise the need to reduce the total allowable catch, they are concerned about how that reduction could impact on their own socio economic livelihoods.

Pedro Garcia: The bigger companies are sitting with 90% of the resources and we know that the big companies can absorb the losses. So what we are saying is take it away from the big companies. You need to deomonstrate the political will in terms of transformation in this country. We are not doing that.

V/O Unemployment and poverty rates are high in Hangberg. Durick van Blerk paid the ultimate price for trying to make a living.

Cleo Adonis: The friday night that he went he was the happiest person ever because he told me that when he comes back this is going to be his last and he is going to be his last because he did not want to do this poaching anymore and he was very excited about the baby.

Up audio: hymn

V/O It has been a few weeks since Durick disappeared at sea. The family still hopes his body will be found so they can lay him to rest.

MacFarlane Moleli: If you could send out a message to Durick what would you say to him?

Edward van Blerk: Daar is niks wat ek vir hom kan se nie, (there is nothing i can say to him) want daar is nie woorde wat ek kan se nie (because there are no words). Jy vra ok maar net, hoekom nou hy? (you can ask, why him?) Hy begin dan nou sy jongman lewe, (he is starting his youngman life) en hy gaan nou n pa raak en nou kan hy nie meer n pa wees nie. Dis moeilik. (and have just become a father and now he can’t be a father any more. It is difficult)
_________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________

Promos:

10 second:
V/O Missing and presumed dead, fisherman Durick van Blerk disappeared at sea after a confrontation with anti-poaching police; will peace ever be restored to Hangberg in Hout Bay?

15 second:
V/O Small scale fishermen of Hangberg depend on the sea for their livelihood but government quotas make it impossible for them to work legally. Now they risk run-ins with anti-poaching police.
Neville Adonis: They go out without a permit to go and catch because they are sick and tired.

15 second:
V/O Poaching has become the only option for many fishers of Hangberg as government runs years behind schedule in issuing small scale fishing licenses.
Ralph Warner: In Hangberg I have got four siblings to support. What must I do? So I turn to poaching.

30 second:
V/O Fisherman Durick van Blerk went missing after allegedly being shot at by police during an anti-poaching raid out at sea near Hout Bay. Frustrations mounted and in anger the fishing community took their protest to the street.
Edward van Blerk: Ek is baie baie ontsteld vir die polisiemanne wat daar was (I am very upset about the police who were there), want die wet se as jy sien n persoon val in die water op see dan moet jy vir hom uit die water help, (because the law says that when you see a person falling in the sea then you have to help him out of the water) jy kan nie net hom daar los nie. (you can’t just leave him there)

Insert in Show: Title Author Last Updated 23 September 2018 - Carte Blanche HD Nikola Vrahimis 26 September 2018 Script: FINAL SCRIPT: Hangberg on a knife’s edge Producer: Annalise Lubbe / Presenter: MacFarlane Moleli Date: 7 September 2018 / Duration: 10 minutes V/O Hangberg, a traditional fishing community in Cape Town. It’s roughly six and a half thousand residents depend on the sea – catching crayfish, abalone and line fish. As the population grew and commercial fishing increased, fish stocks declined. Government efforts to license access to the ocean forced out traditional fishers. Many turned to poaching as a way out. Ralph Warner: Fisher - My father was a fisherman; my grandfather had boats, a lot of rowing dinghies, so they were catching quotas; now where is the quotas now? MacFarlane Moleli: So how does this make you feel? This is your life. Ralph Warner: It’s make me feel sad. In Hangberg I have got four siblings to support. What must I do? So I turn to poaching. V/O In 2005 a civic organisation took government to the equality court over its policies that excluded artisanal fishers. In 2007 the court ruled that interim rights must be given to small-scale fishers. The Department of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries or DAFF had to devise a policy that covered small-scale fishers. By 2012 the new policy was announced – but to date it has not been implemented. In Hangberg only 97 fishers, out of the hundreds in the area, have Interim Relief permits. Neville Adonis: Fisher - You must go and catch the fish but you can’t catch the fish if you haven’t got a permit. I fill in my form, it’s in, come back, unsuccessful. All the fisherman, not me alone, all the fisherman, they are sick and tired. Up natural sound: police shooting and firing rubber bullets. V/O Unable to improve their lives when fishing quotas are poor, residents often protest in frustration over poor living conditions. The municipality has evicted fishers form illegal shacks – the only homes they can afford. There are sporadic and increasing, violent clashes between police and Hangberg residents. Up audio: V/O In August renewed unrest erupted after a 26-year old fisherman Durick van Blerk was allegedly shot at by police. Van Blerk disappeared at the sea. Like so many youngsters in Hangberg, Van Blerk had turned to poaching to try and improve his life. UP audio: so you are looking to start a family now. V/O His fiance, Cleo Adonis, is heavily pregnant. MacFarlane Moleli: So Cleo this your home? Cleo Adonis: Fiance - Yeh. This was the home me and Durick prepared before all this happened. As you can see we are still busy building and sorting out the house before the baby comes. He was very excited to become a dad, this will be his first child. MacFarlane Moleli: What kind of boyfriend was he? Cleo Adonis: He was very loving. He was my everything in my life. If I call him, Durick come and fetch me here. He would come immediately. V/O Van Blerk’s father Edward was helping his son with electrical fittings in his new home. Edward van Blerk: Father - Ek is besig om die huis maarwee hy besig is te help bou (I am busy helping him with the home he was building) Toe het ek vrydag die 10de het ek gegaan, het ek begin nou in die mure die snywerk doen sodat ons die plugs en pype in die muur kan sit. (On Friday the tenth I went there to cut into the walls to install the plugs and pipes) Up audio boat sound V/O That was the last time that Van Blerk saw his son. In the early hours of 11 August Van Blerk and two other men went out crayfishing around Hout Bay – illegally. Police were scouting for poachers – outside of crayfish season anyone in the water was a suspect. The police allegedly fired shots in their direction and Van Blerk went overboard Edward van Blerk: Daar is rumours daar was geskiet maar ons het niks bewyse nie. (there are rumours that shots have been fired) ek is baie baie ontsteld vir die polisiemanne wat daar was (I am very upset about the police who were there), want die wet se as jy sien n persoon val in die water op see dan moet jy vir hom uit die water help, (because the law says that when you see a person falling in the sea then you have to help him out of the water) jy kan nie net hom daar los nie. (you can’t just leave him there) V/O Van Blerk’s two friends were arrested for possession of illegal crayfish and brought to shore. Word got out about the alleged shooting. MacFarlane Moleli: Wat se die ander twee manne van die ding? (What do the other two men say about this?) Edward van Blerk: Die ander twee manne se op die boot van hulle was geskiet. (the other two men said they shot at the boat) Die een persoon se Durick het op hom gaan val (the one person said Durick fell on him) die ander se hy het net gesien Durick is in die water met sy hande in die lug (the other one said he saw Durick was in the water with his hands up in the air) want dit was mos nou donker gewees toe die nou gebeur het. (because it was obviously dark when it happened). V/O When Van Blerk didn’t return from sea his family turned to the police, but they learned nothing about his disappearance. In the days that followed a number of search teams went out, including SAPS divers, the National Sea Rescue Institute and local fishers. Up sound: Link: Due to the anger and frustration of the fishing community they took to the streets in protests and also burnt down some government buildings. This is one of them. V/O Protesters unleashed their anger on the Department of Fisheries – an employee’s house and car, as well as the station master’s office, were set alight. A warehouse was destroyed. Up sound: V/O We asked the police to explain what happened on the night Van Blerk went missing. They said they are not in a position to grant an interview as the Independent Police Investigation Directorate is investigating the police for attempted murder. IPID confirmed this. No arrest has been made yet. MacFarlane Moleli: The reaction of the community is very angry about what has happened to the shooting of one of the fishers. Ralph Warner: Fisher - The people must be angry because we don’t hunt with the gun the crayfish. We go out there to put food on our table. Why do they shoot the people? Why? V/O Pedro Garcia represents small scale fishers on national level. Their primary objective is to restore justice and empower informal fishers. Pedro Garcia: Co-chair Small Scale Collective - In 2007 the court ruled that a small scale policy be developed. It is now 12, 13 years and nothing has happened so you can imagine the frustrations that is on the ground. DAFF had failed our people. Make no mistake about that. They had allocated resources which were critically needed. They have allocated those resources to the bigger companies and to the near shore commercial. V/O DAFF’s Craig Smith is responsible for the Small Scale Fishing policy. MacFarlane Moleli: So Graig we met some small scale fishers that have been fishing all of their lives, they meet all the criteria and they have applied and said nothing has happened. They say the department has led them down. Craig Smith - Director Small Scale Fisheries DAFF: For Western Cape, yes we have experienced delays. We haven’t got to the point of announcing the final list of fishers in western cape. MacFarlane Moleli: When do you think it will be finalised? Craig Smith: We are currently waiting for the minister to make the final decision on the list for western cape. One of the hiccups is with this national implementation the staff component is severely curtailed. We have only 8 staff in DAFF to implement this national programme. MacFarlane Moleli: So would you not say the Department needs to work faster. Craig Smith: There is no doubt that it needs to be expedited. The court case happened in 2007, we are eleven years after that particular court order and certainly we owe it to our communities to implement small scale fishing a lot quicker. V/O Fishing rights only have value as long as there are fish in the sea. But in addition to the limited access to permits, small scale fishers have been dealt another blow. The World Wide Fund is taking DAFF to court over its apparent failure to safeguard the future of the West Coast Rock lobster. Dr. Theressa Frantz is head of their Environmental Programmes. Dr Theressa Frantz - Head Environmental Programmes WWF-SA: We are extremely concerned about the status of the West Coast Rock Lobster resource. The global standard is 20%; we are at 2%. So by any standard we have already depleted this resource. V/O DAFF has set the total allowable catch for South Africa for the West Coast Rock lobster at 1924 tonnes. Scientists say that’s more than double the amount that should be fished if stocks are to stabilise and recover. Dr Theressa Frantz: So WWF is challenging the Department of Agriculture Forestry and Fisheries in court over the deputy director general’s decision for a total allowable catch that far exceeds the scientifically recommended level. The small scale fisheries collective has in fact come out in terms of our application and they understand the reason for sustainability of resource. While they recognise the need to reduce the total allowable catch, they are concerned about how that reduction could impact on their own socio economic livelihoods. Pedro Garcia: The bigger companies are sitting with 90% of the resources and we know that the big companies can absorb the losses. So what we are saying is take it away from the big companies. You need to deomonstrate the political will in terms of transformation in this country. We are not doing that. V/O Unemployment and poverty rates are high in Hangberg. Durick van Blerk paid the ultimate price for trying to make a living. Cleo Adonis: The friday night that he went he was the happiest person ever because he told me that when he comes back this is going to be his last and he is going to be his last because he did not want to do this poaching anymore and he was very excited about the baby. Up audio: hymn V/O It has been a few weeks since Durick disappeared at sea. The family still hopes his body will be found so they can lay him to rest. MacFarlane Moleli: If you could send out a message to Durick what would you say to him? Edward van Blerk: Daar is niks wat ek vir hom kan se nie, (there is nothing i can say to him) want daar is nie woorde wat ek kan se nie (because there are no words). Jy vra ok maar net, hoekom nou hy? (you can ask, why him?) Hy begin dan nou sy jongman lewe, (he is starting his youngman life) en hy gaan nou n pa raak en nou kan hy nie meer n pa wees nie. Dis moeilik. (and have just become a father and now he can’t be a father any more. It is difficult) _________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________ Promos: 10 second: V/O Missing and presumed dead, fisherman Durick van Blerk disappeared at sea after a confrontation with anti-poaching police; will peace ever be restored to Hangberg in Hout Bay? 15 second: V/O Small scale fishermen of Hangberg depend on the sea for their livelihood but government quotas make it impossible for them to work legally. Now they risk run-ins with anti-poaching police. Neville Adonis: They go out without a permit to go and catch because they are sick and tired. 15 second: V/O Poaching has become the only option for many fishers of Hangberg as government runs years behind schedule in issuing small scale fishing licenses. Ralph Warner: In Hangberg I have got four siblings to support. What must I do? So I turn to poaching. 30 second: V/O Fisherman Durick van Blerk went missing after allegedly being shot at by police during an anti-poaching raid out at sea near Hout Bay. Frustrations mounted and in anger the fishing community took their protest to the street. Edward van Blerk: Ek is baie baie ontsteld vir die polisiemanne wat daar was (I am very upset about the police who were there), want die wet se as jy sien n persoon val in die water op see dan moet jy vir hom uit die water help, (because the law says that when you see a person falling in the sea then you have to help him out of the water) jy kan nie net hom daar los nie. (you can’t just leave him there) ____________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________ Invoicing Back references from Insert ID in Invoice: Title Author Last Updated Invoice for Hangberg on a knife's edge (5294) Annalise Lubbe 05 September 2018

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): When a fisher goes missing at sea during a police raid the locals of Hangberg take to the streets in protest. Carte Blanche investigate.
metadata.Summary: It is cold winter’s morning in Hangberg, a fishing village on the outskirts of Hout Bay. From inside the church the last notes of “what a friend we have in Jesus” filters through the somber air. The Pastor prays for the return of a ‘missing son’ and lay hands on the family as they ask for a miracle to happen. It has been five days since Deurick van Blerk went missing at sea. In the icy winter waters of the Cape there is little hope now for a safe return. “Please bring back our son,” ask the father, Edward van Blerk. “We still have hope that we will see our son alive,” he says. 26-Year-old Deurick van Blerk went missing on Friday night when he was out at sea catching crayfish with two fellow fishers. On the same night SAPS Water wing was out in full swing on an anti-poaching operation. They came across the boat, confiscated the crayfish and arrested two of the three fishers. In a statement issued by SAPS they were not clear if Van Blerk fell overboard or jumped. People are now speculating that perhaps he was shot at by the police and fell into the icy Cape waters.
metadata.Further information: On Saturday morning, the NSRI and EMS choppers did a search for van Blerk but were later told to return to land when the weather turned nasty. On the same day Edward van Blerk filed a report for his missing son. He was told by the police that the search will only continue the following day. On Sunday the search continued: the police sent out two jet skis and a rubber duck. “Why did they not send out proper big search boats like the ones they used on Friday night?”, says Ikram Halim, a representative of the Small Scale fishers. They are not serious about the search, he exclaims. The community of Hangberg took to the streets in protest against the feeble attempt by the police. They set alight a fish factory, burned down one of DAFF’s offices and set a fishing boat alight in one of the streets. Eleven people were arrested. On Monday the search continued. On Tuesday it was called off when the rubber duck ran out of petrol. On Wednesday afternoon the family was told that unless they have further leads, they will call of the search this Friday. Behind the veil of protest is anger. Anger about the fact that they have been marginalised as fishers. Almost every second person living in Hangberg is a fisher. Over the years they have lost their quota as small scale fishers and can no longer make a living on what they are allowed to catch. There are about 6 500 people living in Hangberg on the size of a postage stamp: cramped in and nowhere to expand. Most of the men here are fishers and have been living off the sea for generations. But due to DAFF cutting down on the amount of permits issued each year for crayfishing and abalone, cutting out a decent living has become impossible and poaching became the only way out. Poaching is rife in the waters along the coast of Hout Bay. Stretching over several kilometres it is an impossible task to police the waters efficiently. Besides SAPS’ water wing, the City of Cape Town has their own Marine Law Enforcement task team patrolling the waters for illegal fishing activities. On any give clear day you will find poachers. The only way to spot them easily is with a drone. Here about 12 divers is out in full force diving out abalone. But is the solution to work reactively and go after the poachers or should we not look at sustainable solutions that will be beneficial to both the small scale fishers, the commercial companies and most importantly our marine life. Sustainability of our sea resources is vital for job creation: from pro bono fishers to commercial companies, protecting our marine resource is imperative for the future. Scientific studies has shown that the total allowable catch (TAC) for the West Coast rock lobster is at a level which will wipe out the crustaceans if drastic measures are not put in place to cut down the percentage of rock lobsters harvested each year from our seas. The World Wide Fund for Nature South Africa (WWF-SA) is taking the Department of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries (DAFF) to court over its failure to safeguard the future of the special and all the fishers who depend on this valuable resource. Currently less that 2% of its pre-fished stock size, the the west coast rock lobster is in danger to be wiped out. Pedro Garcia, founder of the South African United Fishing Front (SAUFF) have been working with WWF to plead for the sustainable future of the rock lobster as this is directly related to the future of the artisans. Following the protest in Hout Bay, Fisheries minister, Senzeni Zokwana has issued directives to senior officials to accelerate the process of allocating fishing rights in coastal communities. But why has it taken almost 10 years, says Halim, for them to sit up and taken notice? And is this not going to be another ploy to pacify the community when they have not made any serious attempt to help us since 2006. Jacobus van Niekerk has been a fisher for 29 years. Every year his wife, Charmaigne fills in the form requesting for a small scale fishing permit. “I sit in the hall when they call out the names, but his name is never on the list”. “We have given up trying”. Jacobus is now working on a boat to make a living and he is just one of many disappointed fishers who have been sidelined by the government in the issuing of permits. Our Story: We tell the story behind the missing fisher: why poaching has become the only way out for the fishers of Hangberg. We hear from the van Blerk family about losing a son; from the community about losing their dignity and from a poacher resorting to illegal fishing as the only way out. We put the government on the spot and ask why it is taking so long to allocate fishing rights to those who need it most; and hear from SAPS what really happened that night and get a perspective from the WWF on the sustainable future of the rock lobster and how it will impact the small scale fishers.
